## The question

[Can I consider isomophism in graph theory as the term "mapping" as isomorphism in Abstract Algebra?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2442884/can-i-consider-isomophism-in-graph-theory-as-the-term-mapping-as-isomorphism-i), asked by [Lingnoi401](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/353503/lingnoi401) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-09-24; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I just start studying graph theory as found it's weird mathematics area
> I want to learn from math point view ,but when I try to find clip in youtube,mostly mention from com sci point view  ok that is not problem in this question
>

> I just start read a few page of graph theory book I don't know to prove in graph theory term.
> But I borrow the term from group theory(even I don't know operation or the elenment that i define is group or not)
> define group G has order 3 (e,c,d) has operation "draw a line to each element" and do nothing is identity of this group
> and H as order 2 (C',D') as the "do notthing" each elemnt (in this case the i don't know how to define idenitiy)
>
> since order is not equal it can't mapping bijective to each group therefore it's not isomorphism 
> Can I use this similiar proof in isomorphism proof in graph theory ?
:::

There is already a notion from graph theory  related to the thing you are trying to do.  The *degree* of a vertex is defined to be the number of edges that contain that vertex.  A graph isomorphism preserves the degree of each vertex.

In your graphs, $A$ and $B$ have degree 2, while $A'$ and $B'$ have degree 3.  So a mapping which sends $A$ to $A'$, $B$ to $B'$, etc., cannot be an isomorphism.

A more interesting question is whether there exists *any* isomorphism between the two graphs.  For that, I would look at the quadrilateral of degree-3 vertices within the righthand graph.
